opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it felt slow at the time, and I think that's true for a lot of people who work in formal methods. When you're building a solver or proving that some technique is sound, there's no shortcut. You can't just run a quick experiment, see a number go up, and write it up. You have to get every detail right, because the whole point of the field is correctness. One subtle bug in your reasoning or in the implementation and the result means nothing.

So a single paper could take a really long time: a lot of reading, a lot of thinking, a lot of implementation, and a lot of moments where you think you've got it and then realize there's a corner case that breaks everything. Early on, that was frustrating. You look around and see people in other areas putting out several papers a year, and you wonder if you're falling behind.

Looking back, though, I see that time very differently. It trained me to think rigorously, to be patient with hard problems, and to care about whether something is *actually* right rather than whether it looks right. That mindset carried over when I moved into machine learning systems. In systems work, a small mistake in scheduling or memory management can silently cost you a lot of performance or correctness, and having that discipline helped a lot.

The other thing I learned is that progress in research isn't linear. You can spend months feeling stuck, and then things come together in a few weeks. So now, when I mentor students, I tell them not to measure themselves only by paper count, especially early on. The depth you build during those slow periods is often what lets you move fast later.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it took much longer than I expected, and I think that's the normal experience in formal methods rather than the exception. When I started, I assumed the hard part would be having the right idea. In reality the idea was maybe ten percent of the work. The rest was making it actually hold up: pinning down the semantics precisely, getting the proofs to go through in the prover, and discovering over and over that a definition I thought was obviously correct had a corner case I hadn't considered.

There was one paper where I spent close to a year on what I initially estimated as a two-month project. Most of that year wasn't visible progress. It was me realizing that a lemma I depended on was false in a way that only showed up in a tiny edge case, and then having to restructure a big chunk of the development around it. That's painful in the moment, but it's also exactly why you do formal methods. The whole point is that the machine doesn't let you hand-wave.

So I've stopped thinking of that time as slowness or wasted effort. Every one of those long stretches was the proof assistant teaching me something I didn't actually understand yet. If anything, the fact that it took a long time is a sign the problem was real. The papers that come together quickly tend to be the ones where you already knew the answer, and those usually aren't the interesting ones.

The other thing I'd say is that the time compounds. Each project felt like it would take forever, but the tooling, the proof libraries, and my own intuition for how to structure a formalization all carried over. The second and third papers were faster not because the problems were easier, but because I'd already paid for a lot of the infrastructure, both in code and in my own head.

astra-6.text: Looking back, I think a lot of the time was spent figuring out what the right question was. With formal methods, you can have an idea that sounds reasonable, but making the assumptions precise and showing that it actually works takes time. So progress didn’t always look like progress day to day. Sometimes it meant realizing why an approach wouldn’t work, and that understanding was what made the next step possible.

sol-6.1.text: Looking back, I think that time was part of learning how to do research. With formal methods, you can spend a long time just figuring out how to formulate the problem precisely. You try an approach, discover why it doesn’t work, and then understand the problem a little better. That doesn’t always look like progress, because you don’t have a paper yet, but it’s still progress. Of course, when you’re in the middle of it, it can feel frustrating. It’s much easier to see the value of that time afterward.
